title: How Spring finds an annotation you never wrote
summary: From a class reference to a merged, alias-resolved annotation instance. The whole thing is a graph walk plus an attribute mapping table, cached hard because it runs constantly at startup.
entry: Put a breakpoint in AnnotationTypeMapping.getMirrorSets and start any Spring app. It fires while the container is reading your stereotypes.

steps.notice: The entry point everything else in Spring funnels through. Note the SearchStrategy parameter: DIRECT, INHERITED_ANNOTATIONS, SUPERCLASS, TYPE_HIERARCHY. Picking the wrong one is the usual reason an annotation is silently ignored.
Walks the element according to the strategy: the element itself, then superclasses, then interfaces. This is the part that decides WHERE to look, before anything is merged.
Builds the meta-annotation graph for one annotation type: @ServiceEndpoint to @Service to @Component, breadth first. Heavily cached, because this is pure computation over types that never change.

Where @AliasFor actually lives. A mirror set is a group of attributes that must agree; resolving one picks the single declared value or throws if two disagree. Read this and both jobs of @AliasFor make sense at once.
Reads an attribute through the mapping, so a value declared on the outer annotation surfaces on the meta-annotation. This is why @GetMapping("/x") sets @RequestMapping's path.
synthesize() hands back a JDK proxy implementing the annotation interface, not the annotation the compiler produced. That is how merged values reach code that just calls annotation.value().

The legacy API, still everywhere. Compare its synthesize(AnnotationUtils::isSingleLevelPresent) with findAnnotation's synthesize(MergedAnnotation::isPresent): getAnnotation stops one meta-level out, findAnnotation does not. Same-looking calls, different reach.
